Fit a mortality model by maximum weighted log-likelihood

Source: R/fit.R
fit.Rd

Estimates the coefficients of a model() against experience data, by Newton-Raphson on the weighted log-likelihood $$L^* = \Omega^{-1}(\mathrm{A}w\log\mu - \mathrm{E}w).$$

A fit returns a fit or it fails. A model that does not converge, or whose information matrix cannot be factored, raises an error carrying the diagnosis rather than returning a number nobody should use.

Usage

fit(
  exp_data,
  model,
  include = NULL,
  weight = NULL,
  val_relevance = NULL,
  val_distance = NULL,
  test_mortality = default_mortality(),
  Z = NULL,
  settings = NULL,
  overdispersion = NULL,
  time_scale = NULL,
  start = NULL,
  L_tolerance = default_L_tolerance,
  armijo = default_armijo,
  max_iterations = default_max_iterations,
  max_halvings = default_max_halvings,
  threads = cpp_veil_default_threads()
)

is_fit(x)

Arguments

exp_data

The experience data.

model

The model() to fit.

include

An include restricting the population, or NULL for all of it.

weight

A pronoun expression for the weight \(w\), or NULL for lives. Weights must not be negative.

val_relevance, val_distance

A pronoun expression for the second weighting factor, in either spelling. At most one may be given.

test_mortality

The mortality on which the \(Z\) scale is measured. See Details.

Z

The \(Z\) scale as a single positive number, given instead of a test_mortality rather than as well as one.

settings

A settings() object carrying overdispersion and time_scale.

overdispersion, time_scale

Given directly, these override the settings.

start

Starting coefficients, one per model term. Defaults to zeros.

L_tolerance

The convergence tolerance, as a gain in \(L\). One unit of \(L\) is about what one parameter costs.

armijo

The fraction of the linearly predicted gain a damped step must actually deliver to be accepted. Must lie strictly between 0 and 0.5.

max_iterations

The most Newton steps to take.

max_halvings

The most times one step may be halved before the fit is abandoned.

threads

The number of worker threads.

x, object

A fit.

...

Ignored.

Value

fit() returns a fit, whose fields are beta, mortality (the fitted model as a mortality), variance, L, p, L_P, Z, overdispersion, population (the population and test-mortality numbers print() reports), arguments (the include, weight and relevance the fit was run with, kept so that diagnose() can reuse them), labels (what was written for the include, the weight and the test mortality), iterations, evaluations, predicted_gain and model.

is_fit() returns a scalar logical.

coef() returns the fitted coefficients as a named numeric vector, and vcov() their variance-covariance matrix.

residuals() stops with a message: a fit keeps no data, so residuals come from an aev() on the fitted mortality.

summary() returns a summary.fit: the coefficients table (estimate, std_error for one standard deviation and conf_95pc for the 95% half-width), the correlation matrix of the estimates, and the header's numbers. A fit prints as its summary.

The Z scale

Results are reported on the \(L = Z^{-1}L^*\) scale, where \(Z = \mathrm{E}w^2/\mathrm{E}w\) on a test mortality. \(Z\) is a change of units, chosen so that one parameter costs about one unit of \(L\), and it must be the same for every model being compared – otherwise the penalised log-likelihoods are not on one scale and the comparison means nothing.

It is set in one of two ways, never from the model's own reference mortality, and they are alternatives rather than a pair:

  • test_mortality names the mortality \(Z\) is measured on, over this same data, weight and include. It defaults to default_mortality(), and a fixed shared choice is worth more here than a good one, since \(Z\)'s job is to be one yardstick.

  • Z gives \(Z\) directly as a number, skipping the measurement. This is what model selection needs, the caller having obtained it once and passed it to every candidate, and compare_models() does exactly that.

Where the weight is absent, is the literal 1, or takes only the values 0 and 1 – a logical expression, or a column holding nothing but zeros and ones – \(w^2 = w\) makes \(Z\) exactly one. The engine recognises such a weight and accumulates \(\mathrm{E}w^2\) as \(\mathrm{E}w\) itself, so the measured \(Z\) is one to the last bit rather than to a tolerance. The measurement is made regardless, since the same pass over the data supplies the population figures that print() reports.

Convergence

The iteration stops when the gain in \(L\) still available falls below L_tolerance, which is a forward-looking test: it measures the distance left to the optimum rather than the size of the last step, so it is not fooled by a damped step or by a model whose maximum does not exist. Stopping within \(\epsilon\) of the maximum leaves the coefficients within \(\sqrt{2\epsilon/I}\) of theirs.

Examples

data <- exp_data(
  list(
    birth     = datey::datey(c(1945, 1950, 1955, 1940, 1948)),
    male      = c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE),
    E2R_start = datey::datey(rep(2015, 5)),
    E2R_end   = datey::datey(c(2020, 2020, 2018, 2020, 2019)),
    E2R_died  = c(FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)
  ),
  exp_start = datey::datey(2015),
  exp_end   = datey::datey(2020)
)

m <- model(ref_mortality = gompertz_mortality(), covariates = covariates(level = 1))
fit(data, m, settings = settings(overdispersion = 1))
#> <fit: 1 term, 5 iterations, 6 walks of the data>
#>   include         all records
#>   weight          lives
#>   data            2 deaths, 22 years of exposure
#>   test mortality  logmu default
#>                   Aw 2   Ew 0.36215   Ew^2 0.36215   Z 1
#>                   log A/E 1.7088 ± 1.6617 (1 sd) or ± 3.2569 (95%), at overdispersion 1
#>   overdispersion  1
#> 
#>       estimate std_error conf_95pc
#> level    1.709    0.7071     1.386
#> 
#> L -7.752328   p 1   L_P -8.752328   k 1
